chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ahmad ibn Muhammad said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about what is killed by the dog and the cheetah. He said, 'Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: The dog and the cheetah are the same. If it takes it and holds it, and dies while holding it, then eat it, for it has held it for you. And if it holds it and eats from it, then do not eat, for it has held it for itself.' And what we previously mentioned regarding that what is killed by the cheetah is not permissible to eat in any state, that is the practice upon it. And what comes from the narrations regarding the permissibility of that is subject to two interpretations: one is that they are based on a type of precautionary piety (tawqiyyah), because the rulers of the time employed cheetahs for hunting, so they did not forbid it in that regard. And the second is that they are based on the state of necessity, because in the case of necessity, it is permissible to eat from what the cheetah has killed. And the narration previously mentioned regarding the permissibility of that is from al-Rida (peace be upon him), and he also narrated.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating game killed by a hunting dog or cheetah if it eats from the prey?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of hunting by distinguishing between a beast that merely holds its prey (permissible) versus one that consumes it (impermissible), a distinction rooted in the concept of 'holding' as a form of slaughter. Al-Tusi provides scholarly reconciliation for conflicting reports by attributing them to *tawqiyyah* (precautionary piety, given rulers' use of cheetahs) or *idtirar* (necessity), demonstrating the flexibility of Shia legal methodology in reconciling apparent contradictions.
